claims.text: Namakkal Maakkal Pattirangal is a traditional category of stone utensils, domestic wares, ritual objects, toys and carved articles made from soapstone native to Namakkal district.

quotes.quote: Namaakkal Maakkal Pattirangal refers to a traditional category of stone utensils, domestic wares, ritual objects, toys, and carved articles produced from the distinctive soapstone deposits native to the Namaakkal district of Tamil Nadu.
Locally known as "Maakkal," these stone vessels and artefacts are carved from a soft yet durable variety of soapstone

claims.text: Tamil Nadu soapstone vessels are suited to storing milk, curd and buttermilk and are preferred for cooking dishes made with tamarind and lime.

quotes.quote: Utilitarian stoneware of the highest excellence is made in Salem district and in the region between Pondicherry and Cudallore in Tamil Nadu.
Utensils made of soapstone, which is a soft light gray colour with a cool smooth texture, are perfectly suited to store buttermilk, milk and curds.
It is also the preferred vessel for cooking food that uses tamarind and lime.
the kalchatti is considered the best cookware for the fiery local curries spiced with tamarind and lime that need a slow long cook to release flavors
Their slow, even heat distribution makes them especially suited for preparing tamarind- and lime-based gravies such as puli kozhambu, moru kulambu, and various regional buttermilk dishes.
are an excellent medium for cooking tamarind based dishes and are ideal to store pickles, milk and curd

claims.text: Tamil Nadu soapstone wares include kalchatti cooking pots, dosa pans, food moulds, storage jars, serving dishes, and mortars and pestles.

quotes.quote: The culinary utensils produced under Namaakkal Maakkal Pattirangal include Kalchattis (stone cooking pots), dosa pans, kuzhi paniyaram moulds, storage jars with lids, curd and buttermilk pots, pickle jars, rolling pins, and serving vessels.

Differently sized kalchattis form mortars and pestles for grinding lentils, grains and spices, storage containers to food moulds, cooking utensils, serving dishes, and pans for the local bread (dosa) are crafted.
The items made are vessels for storage, serving dishes, mortar and pestle, bowls and ornamented single-wick lamps.
Utilitarian stoneware of the highest excellence is made in Salem district and in the region between Pondicherry and Cudallore in Tamil Nadu.

Apart from cookwares like dosa pan, vessel, 'kuzhipaniyaram' plates, the artisans from this region also chisel out lamps, idols, incense stands, candle stands, paperweights, toys and miniature figurines.

claims.text: Namakkal artisans also make idols, sirpangal sculptures, incense and candle stands, star-shaped Natchatra Vilakku lamps, Kondai Vilakku lamps and miniature figurines.

quotes.quote: the artisans produce a variety of ritual and aesthetic objects including idols, sirpangal (sculptures), incense stands, candle stands, Natchatra Vilakku (star-shaped lamps), Kondai Vilakku, paperweights, miniature figurines

claims.text: The GI application says Namakkal is especially renowned for soapstone dolls and toys called choppu, miniature household items often used in children's play sets and Golu displays.

quotes.quote: Namaakkal is especially renowned for its soapstone dolls and toys, locally known as choppu, which are popular across Tamil Nadu and India.
These miniature representations of household items and cultural motifs are often used in traditional children's play sets and festival displays, particularly during Golu celebrations.

claims.text: Namakkal soapstone is described as a soft, dense metamorphic rock formed by alteration of pre-existing rocks under heat, pressure and reactive fluids, enriching it with talc.

quotes.quote: Namaakkal stone works are crafted from high-quality soapstone, a naturally soft, dense, and easily workable metamorphic rock formed through the alteration of pre- existing rocks under intense heat, pressure, and the activity of chemically reactive fluids in tectonic plate zones.
This slow geological transformation enriches the stone with talc and other minerals

claims.text: IANS reported that Namakkal families carve kalchattis and other cookware from a distinctive magnesium-rich, velvet-smooth soapstone.

quotes.quote: For generations, families in and around Namakkal have carved kalchattis and other cookware from a distinctive magnesium-rich, velvet-smooth soapstone

claims.text: Namakkal soapstone is described as naturally resistant to corrosion by acids, alkalis, salts and citrus compounds.

quotes.quote: The soapstone used for Namaakkal Maakkal Pattirangal is naturally resistant to the corrosive effects of acids, alkalis, salts, and citrus compounds.
the stone is unsusceptible to corrosion by acids and alkalis

claims.text: Soapstone cookware is described as a good insulator that distributes heat evenly and retains warmth long after it is removed from the stove.

quotes.quote: the stone is a strong thermal insulator capable of distributing heat evenly and retaining warmth long after being removed from the stove.
The benefit of cooking in soapstone utensils is that they are good insulators and can retain heat for longer as compared to other metals and clay utensils.
The soapstone, known for its hot and cold insulative properties

claims.text: The GI application describes the soapstone as having low water absorption, so that it does not retain moisture.

quotes.quote: The stone exhibits inherently low water absorption capacity, ensuring that it does not retain moisture
possess low water absorption ability

claims.text: New soapstone vessels look light grey, but repeated use, oil absorption and heat turn their surface darker and smoother.

quotes.quote: New vessels appear light grey, but with repeated use, oil absorption and heat exposure gradually transform them into a darker, smoother, and visually richer surface

claims.text: The GI application describes Namakkal stone utensils as keeping a rough, porous, naturally textured surface, unlike the polished, lathe-finished soapstone utensils of Keonjhar in Odisha.

quotes.quote: A signature characteristic of Namaakkal Maakkal Pattirangal is their rough, porous, and naturally textured surface.
Unlike polished and lathe-finished soapstone utensils produced in regions like Keonjhar, Odisha, the Namaakkal utensils retain a rough, porous, naturally textured surface
They have a rough and porous surface and texture, which is a unique feature of the Namakkal makkal stone work as against the usual polished surfaces of other soapstone products

claims.text: The GI application says Namakkal artisans carve each utensil from a single block of stone by visual judgement, without templates, measurements or mechanical aids.

quotes.quote: Each utensil, lamp, idol, or toy is carved from a single block of stone using traditional tools such as uli, olaiuli, yetrauli, and thawttuuli.
Artisans do not use templates, measurements, or mechanical aids; instead, they depend solely on their visual judgment and ancestral skills passed down across generations

claims.text: Patthar Kundo turning needs two craftsmen: one pulls a rope to roll the axis clockwise and anticlockwise while the other carves the stone with carving tools.

while the another craftsman preforms stone carving process, with the help of different carving tools.

claims.text: The lathe bases are a pair of notched and grooved hardwood blocks fixed into the sand base of a clay floor.

quotes.quote: A pair of two differently notched and grooved hard wood blocks. These blocks are getting fixed into sand base of clay floor.

claims.text: The turning axis bar is a hardwood cylinder with a round iron tail, and the raw stone block is fixed to its head with melted Kulsum glue.

quotes.quote: A hard wood, cylindrical bar with a head and round iron tail. This tool is used to fix raw stone block over its head component, using melted Kulsum glue.

claims.text: A Y-shaped wooden turning base helps the turner keep the tool balanced while turning.

quotes.quote: A "Y" shaped wooden structure. Helps turner to make 'balance of tool', during turning process

claims.text: The Patthar Kundo turning tool has a sharp iron tip and a rounded wooden handle and carves the soapstone block as it turns.

quotes.quote: A turning tool, made up of sharptip iron, with rounded wooden handle. Carve the soapstone block, during turning process.

claims.text: A leg stopper helps the rope-pulling craftsperson keep the axis rolling at an equal speed.

quotes.quote: The 'Leg Stopper', supports ropepulling craftsperson to maintain equal axis rolling speed.

claims.text: Jha found that Patthar Kundo needs no raw material for gripping the stone and, although contemporary turning machines are faster, accurate and precise, wastes less raw material than them.

quotes.quote: The most appealing and unique feature, noticed by this researcher in Patthar Kundo system is, 'zero raw material requirement for head griping purposes'.
Usually today's contemporary turning process machines require a countable amount of pre-sized head-jaw grips to perform its turning process.

However, these systems are faster, accurate, and precise with advanced technology, but still the traditional mechanism of Patthar Kundo proves its precedence over them, in terms of less raw material wastages

claims.text: Jha lists other features of the Patthar Kundo system: a comparatively low installation cost, portability, simple operation and a repairable wooden structure.

quotes.quote: Among other unique features of Patthar Kundo system- comparatively lower installation cost, portability, simplicity in operational mechanism, re-installable and component wise repairable wooden structure.

claims.text: Before turning, craftsmen cut a cubical soapstone block with an extra margin on every side to reduce unexpected edge chipping, then trim the edges by careful chiselling.

to reduce the rate of any unexpected edge chippings and subjected object's damages during craftsmanship

claims.text: Jha divides Patthar Kundo into 18 stages that run in sequence from procuring soapstone at nearby mines to the final product.

claims.text: The shaped stone is cleaned and heated before Kulsum glue is applied to the turning-bar head, and heated again before turning to strengthen the glue bond.

claims.text: The outer and then the inner side of the glued soapstone are turned, heating after turning releases the turned form from the glue, and the form then goes for hand-cutting and finishing.

quotes.quote: Stage-J: Turning of outer side of Kulsum glued soapstone.
Stage-K: Turning of inner side of Kulsum glued soapstone.
Stage-L: Post-turning heating process, to un-glue the turned form.
Stage-N: A post-turned soapstone form, forwarded for hand-cutting and finishing stage.

lede.text: This family takes in soapstone utensils, lathe-turned stoneware, gemstone cutting and polishing, and grinding stones, which continue in use in contemporary Indian traditions among sedentary farmers, pastoral nomads and urban dwellers.

In Namakkal district of Tamil Nadu, Namakkal Maakkal Pattirangal is a traditional category of stone utensils, domestic wares, ritual objects, toys and carved articles made from the district's native soapstone.
In Dhakotha in Kendujhar district of Odisha, Patthar Kundo craftsmen turn soapstone utensils on a rope-pulled wooden lathe that needs two craftsmen.
Grinding stones include the ran-thok rotary quern and ling-chhom nutting stone of the Shertukpens, and the sil battas made in Jhansi and by hand in Delhi.

sentences.text: Grinding stones are among the most ubiquitous artefacts at Southern Neolithic sites in peninsular India, and the Neolithic site of Budihal in Karnataka, dated to about 2480-1580 BCE, has yielded sandstone grinding stones.
Soviet scholars dated the introduction of rotary querns to Central Asia, including India, to the 3rd and 4th centuries CE.
According to the GI application, by the 18th century communities had begun making household articles and kitchenware as well as sculptures from soapstone.
The Shertukpens have a long tradition of making stone tools to grind cereals such as wheat, maize and millet.

Villagers reported that the use of Shertukpen grinding stones had declined due to access to commercially produced flour and mechanical mills, and changing food habits have limited it to remote villages.
At the time of Jha's 2010-2011 study, soapstone carving had existed in Dhakotha for around 55-60 years and may be treated as newer than the traditional Patthar Kundo craft.
The GI application lists the stages as raw material selection, primary cutting, shaping, hollowing, detailing, smoothening, colour uniforming, finishing, seasoning of cookware and final inspection.

The GI application says Namakkal artisans carve each utensil from a single block of stone by visual judgement, and utensil interiors are hollowed gradually with the yetrauli while the wall thickness is checked often.
Sources differ on the lathe: EC-APR reports kalchattis of Thandankoundanpalayam shaped on a lathe, while the GI application says Namakkal utensils are carved without mechanical aids.
Before use, a kalchatti is seasoned by filling it repeatedly with warm rice starch water, which strengthens the stone and prevents cracking on first heating.
Patthar Kundo turning needs two craftsmen, one pulling the rope that rolls the axis and the other carving the stone, which is fixed to the turning bar with heated Kulsum glue.
Stone slabs are first made into pillar-like pieces, which are turned on an electric lathe and then smoothed with sandpaper.
Shertukpen zyopo make grinding stones by collecting raw materials, processing and finishing, and makers said a ran-thok took one month if two to four men worked on it.
Traditional basalt grinding-stone making in India begins with sourcing basalt and quarrying blocks, then knaps them by indirect percussion with iron chisels and hammers.

Sources differ on supply: the GI application says quarries near Semmarapatti continue to supply most of the district's requirements, while IANS reported in December 2025 that Namakkal artisans say easily accessible deposits have largely been exhausted.
Namakkal soapstone is traditionally sourced from Namakkal district and from neighbouring areas such as Periyasoragai and Aranganur in Salem district.
Several soapstone mines around Dhakotha make the cluster self-dependent for raw material, and its craftsmen use blackish grey, pink, orange, light green and dark green soapstone.
Soft granite is not suitable for carving but is ideal for Patthar Kundo, and to meet specific client requirements it is procured from Chennai in Tamil Nadu.
Shertukpen makers collect ling-say, or gneiss, from their surroundings for grinding stones.
The stones the Jhansi shilpkars work include Jhansi red granite, marble and Sajjar stone.
Global InCH says sange-rathek, a dark-brown stone with yellow spots from around Jhansi, is made into lamp-shades, incense-stick stands and small medicine-grinders.
New soapstone vessels look light grey, but repeated use, oil absorption and heat turn their surface darker and smoother.
Tamil Nadu soapstone wares include kalchatti cooking pots, dosa pans, food moulds, storage jars, serving dishes, and mortars and pestles.
The GI application describes Namakkal stone utensils as keeping a rough, porous, naturally textured surface, unlike the polished, lathe-finished soapstone utensils of Keonjhar.
On average, the ran-thok's stationary lower stone, the uukhu, is 40cm across and 10cm thick, and its upper stone, the getheng, is 40cm across and 15cm thick.
Small household chakkis are operated by two people, while larger community or commercial ones use livestock to turn the upper stone.
Patthar Kundo craftspeople make utensils primarily targeted to the dining space and oil lamps, a product with religious importance.
Namakkal Maakkal Paattirangal was advertised as GI application 880 in Geographical Indications Journal 207 dated July 31, 2025, and the registry shows it as registered.

Sources differ on the applicant: the journal names the Tamil Nadu Handicrafts Development Corporation, while the registry names the Namakkal Stone Products Manufacturers Association and the MSME Technology Development Centre.
The Hindu reported that Poompuhar first applied for the GI tag in 2013 and withdrew the application in November 2019.
In December 2025 IANS reported Namakkal artisans saying the GI tag had done little to address the steady depletion of high-quality soapstone, while demand from large retail outlets had risen.
Consumers in the Indian subcontinent prefer chakki-milled flour for its taste and texture but tend to consume more mechanically milled flour because it is cheaper and easily available.
A Jhansi sil batta maker said sales had dropped a lot as mixer-grinders became available.
